Basic Cleaning (Missing Values + Duplicates)¶

In [77]:
# Remove duplicate rows
df = df.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)

# Split numeric / categorical
num_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns.tolist()
cat_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'category']).columns.tolist()

# Fill missing numeric values with median
for c in num_cols:
    df[c] = df[c].fillna(df[c].median())

# Fill missing categorical values with mode
for c in cat_cols:
    if df[c].isnull().any():
        df[c] = df[c].fillna(df[c].mode().iloc[0])

print("Missing values after cleaning:")
print(df.isnull().sum())

Histograms (first 6 numeric columns)¶

In [78]:
sns.set(style="whitegrid")

plot_cols = num_cols[:6]  # To keep it simple

for c in plot_cols:
    plt.figure(figsize=(6,3))
    sns.histplot(df[c], kde=True)
    plt.title(f"Histogram of {c}")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

===============================================================================================================================================================

Interpretations:¶

(1) user_id: This histogram will look almost uniform because user IDs are just identifiers. There is no pattern or trend here. It only shows that all users are included once.

(2) age: The age distribution shows how many people fall into each age group. If the bars are higher around a certain range (example: early 20s), that means most participants are around that age. It helps us understand which age group is most represented in the dataset.

(3) daily_screen_time_hours: This shows how many hours people spend on screens each day. If the graph is skewed to the right, it means most people spend fewer hours on screens. If the bars are higher on the right, it means many participants spend a lot of time on screens daily.

(4) phone_usage_hours: This shows the distribution of daily phone usage. If the bars are tall around 3–5 hours, for example, then that is the common usage range. It helps us see whether people depend more on phones compared to other devices.

(5) laptop_usage_hours: This shows how much time people spend using laptops. If many bars appear in the lower range, it means people use laptops less frequently. If the distribution is higher toward 4–6 hours, it means a lot of participants use laptops regularly, possibly for work or study.

(6) tablet_usage_hours: This histogram shows whether tablets are commonly used. Usually, the bars might be low, meaning fewer people use tablets daily. If the distribution is almost flat or near zero, it means tablets are not used much among participants.

Correlation Heatmap (first 10 numeric columns)¶

In [79]:
corr_cols = num_cols[:10]

plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))
sns.heatmap(df[corr_cols].corr(), annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="vlag", center=0)
plt.title("Correlation Heatmap")
plt.show()

===============================================================================================================================================================

Interpretations:¶

The heatmap shows how the first 10 numeric values are related to each other. Red means a positive relationship (when one goes up, the other also goes up). Blue means a negative relationship (when one increases, the other decreases). Light colors mean there is almost no relationship. Overall, it helps us quickly see which factors move together and which ones do not.

plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))
plt.scatter(y_test, y_pred_test, alpha=0.6)
plt.plot([y_test.min(), y_test.max()], [y_test.min(), y_test.max()], linestyle='--')
plt.xlabel("Actual")
plt.ylabel("Predicted")
plt.title(f"Actual vs Predicted ({target})")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This graph compares the real stress levels (Actual) with the values predicted by the model (Predicted).

  • If the points lie close to the diagonal dashed line, it means the model is predicting well.
  • If the points are scattered far away from the line, it means the model is not very accurate.

# Compares stress levels between City and Rural students.

df["location_type"] = df["location_type"].str.strip()

urban = df[df["location_type"] == "Urban"]["stress_level"].dropna()
rural = df[df["location_type"] == "Rural"]["stress_level"].dropna()

from scipy import stats
tstat, pval = stats.ttest_ind(urban, rural, equal_var=False)

print("T-test (Urban vs Rural stress):")
print("t-stat:", round(tstat, 3))
print("p-value:", round(pval, 4))

print("\nCounts:")
print("Urban count:", len(urban))
print("Rural count:", len(rural))

===============================================================================================================================================================

Daily Scren Time Interpretations:¶

(1) Daily Screen Time vs Stress Level: As daily screen time increases, stress levels also seem to increase. The points are not perfectly aligned, but the trend shows that people who spend more hours on screens tend to report higher stress. The correlation value also supports this.

(2) Daily Screen Time vs Mental Health Score: Higher screen time is linked to lower mental health scores. This means that too much screen time might negatively affect mental well-being. The scatter plot shows a slight downward pattern, and the correlation confirms this.

Interpretations on relation with Total Tech Usage¶

(1) Total Tech Usage vs Sleep Quality: People who spend more total hours on phones, laptops, and gaming tend to have slightly lower sleep quality. The graph shows that sleep quality goes down when tech use goes up. This means excessive tech use might disturb sleep.

(2) Total Tech Usage vs Mood Rating: Mood ratings decrease as total tech usage increases. This suggests that spending too much time on technology may impact mood in a negative way. The relationship isn’t extremely strong, but the trend is visible.

Interpretation on Stress Levels¶

(1) Physical Activity vs Stress Level: As physical activity increases, stress levels tend to decrease. People who exercise more hours per week show lower stress. This supports the idea that physical activity helps reduce stress.

(2) Caffeine Intake vs Stress Level: Higher caffeine intake seems to be connected with higher stress levels. The plot shows a slight upward trend, meaning people who drink more caffeine may feel more stressed.

(3) Boxplot - Stress Levels Across Living Environments: Different living environments have different stress levels. For example, people living in cities might have higher stress than those in rural areas (this depends on your actual output). The boxplot shows how stress values vary within each environment type.
